extracted.intended_audience: labor & employment lawyers, employers, unions, regulators, and policymakers engaged with joint-employer analysis and NLRA rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria for determining joint-employer status (primarily under the NLRA) and related considerations about rulemaking, bargaining obligations, and regulatory/precedential limits. Includes circuit tests, statutory/regulatory distinctions (e.g., FLSA, H-2A), and procedural/impact considerations under the APA and regulatory flexibility statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual exercise requirement for bargaining duty
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint employer's bargaining obligation should be triggered only upon its actual exercise of substantial direct and immediate control over the essential terms and conditions of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board has authority to define duty to bargain in the joint-employer context provided it 'stays within common-law limits'—i.e., trigger duty only when there is actual exercise of substantial direct and immediate control over essential terms and conditions. (See discussion at citation 466.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reservation or authority to control without exercise is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding that one entity is a joint employer should not be based exclusively on a never-exercised contractual reservation of right to control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedent (e.g., Singer) does not support finding joint-employer status based solely on a contractual reservation of rights; authority 'to control' that is never exercised is not a substitute for actual control. The H-2A regulatory context is a limited exception based on regulatory duties, not mere contractual reservation. (Citations: opening paragraphs, discussion at 464.)

rubrics_metrics.name: First Circuit multi-factor emphasis on manner and means
rubrics_metrics.description: First Circuit examines fifteen factors 'to be weighed in their totality' with emphasis on the extent to which the putative joint employer controls the manner and means by which the worker completes tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to determine joint-employer relationship by focusing on the putative joint employer's control over how work is performed. (Case: Casey, 807 F.3d at 405; citation 458.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Circuit 'share significant control' test
rubrics_metrics.description: Second Circuit asks whether two or more entities 'share significant control' over the same employees, using thirteen non-exhaustive factors and focusing on the extent to which control was exercised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single factor is decisive; emphasis on actual exercise of control. (Case: Felder, 27 F.4th at 843-844; citation 458.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Circuit focus on payer/hiring/supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: Third Circuit focuses on which entity paid workers' salaries, hired and fired them, and had control over their daily employment activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include assignments, direct supervision, site-specific training, providing equipment, and verifying hours worked. (Case: Faush, 808 F.3d at 216; citation 458.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Fifth Circuit 'hybrid' test
rubrics_metrics.description: Fifth Circuit applies a hybrid test focusing on the right to hire, fire, supervise, and set work schedules, and on which entity paid the employee's salary, withheld taxes, provided benefits, and set the terms and conditions of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to determine joint-employer status even where contractual rights exist but were exercised only in limited ways. (Case: Perry, 990 F.3d at 928-929; citation 458.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sixth Circuit 'share or codetermine' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Sixth Circuit asks whether two entities share or codetermine matters governing essential terms and conditions, examining a putative joint employer's exercise of ability to hire, fire or discipline, affect compensation and benefits, and direct and supervise performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Case: EEOC v. Skanska USA Building, Inc., 550 Fed. Appx. 253; citation 458.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventh Circuit five-factor test
rubrics_metrics.description: Seventh Circuit applies five factors: (1) extent of control and supervision (incl. scheduling and manner and means), (2) kind of occupation and nature of skill (incl. whether skills are obtained in the workplace), (3) responsibility for costs of operation (equipment, supplies, fees, workplace), (4) method/form of payment and benefits, and (5) length of job commitment/expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court 'looks to see whether the putative employer exercised sufficient control.' (Case: Frey, 903 F.3d at 676-678; citation 458.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Ninth Circuit focus on extent of control over details
rubrics_metrics.description: Ninth Circuit focuses on 'the extent of control that one may exercise over the details of the work of the other' with no one factor being decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis is fact-specific and does not treat any single factor as dispositive. (Case: Global Horizons, 915 F.3d at 638; citation 458.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenth Circuit 'share or codetermine' significant-control test
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenth Circuit applies the 'share or codetermine' standard and looks to whether both entities exercised significant control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Case: Adams v. C3 Pipeline Constr. Inc., 30 F.4th 943, 961; citation 458.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: independent-contractor tests vs joint-employer inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Employee-or-independent-contractor tests are not equivalent to joint-employer tests; relying on independent-contractor precedent to set joint-employer standards is inappropriate beyond points about necessary control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Browning-Ferris and other authorities caution against conflating the two inquiries; joint-employer analysis has a second step asking who exercises control, when, and how. (Citation 499, discussion at 453 and 462.)

rubrics_metrics.name: FLSA/economic-realities standard is broader
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the FLSA the joint-employer doctrine is not limited by common-law agency principles; courts applying the FLSA use an economic-realities approach that may encompass a broader swath of workers than common law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic-realities components focus on who paid salary, withheld taxes, provided benefits, and set terms and conditions; cases (e.g., Salinas, citing Darden) support broader FLSA reach. (Citation 457 and 462-463.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory-context exception (H-2A) to actual-exercise limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: In the H-2A guest worker context, regulations define 'employer' to include entities that 'may hire, pay, fire, supervise or otherwise control' and impose regulatory duties (housing, meals, transportation) such that power to control—even if never exercised—can render an entity a joint employer as to certain matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EEOC v. Global Horizons involved H-2A regulations that expand employment relationship scope; the court's statement about power to control was shaped by those regulatory obligations and did not base joint-employer finding on mere contractual reservation. (Citation 464.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect influence vs mandatory directives (parent/subsidiary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect corporate influence (recommendations, suggested salary ranges, performance forms, best practices) is insufficient to impose joint-employer status absent evidence that the parent's actions amounted to mandatory directions rather than mere recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enterprise Rent-A-Car held parent not a joint employer where subsidiaries had discretion to adopt or disregard recommendations; need mandatory directions to establish joint-employer under FLSA context. (Citation 463.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-step inquiry: who, when, and how exercises control
rubrics_metrics.description: After establishing control over workers, joint-employer cases require answering who is exercising that control, when it was exercised, and how it was exercised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'vital second step' distinguishes joint-employer cases from mere identification of control and is emphasized in Browning-Ferris. (Citation 499.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise of control as 'guiding indicator' in Title VII cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Title VII precedent emphasizes that exercise of control is the 'guiding indicator' for determining employment/joint-employer relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title VII cases (e.g., Felder) require allegations of significant control over the manner and means of work to plausibly assert employment relationships. (Citation 462.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of 'essential terms and conditions'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'essential terms and conditions of employment' is open to interpretation; inclusion of items like 'tenure of employment, including hiring and discharge' can significantly broaden the joint-employer inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguity about what counts as essential terms risks expanding joint-employer status to entities (e.g., general contractors) that have only indirect influence; practical and doctrinal implications must be considered. (Citation 498.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint-employer status can bind non-signatories to collective-bargaining agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts have held that a non-signatory joint employer may be bound by a collective-bargaining agreement signed by the direct employer and a union, creating potential duties to bargain and exposure to liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited show §301 LMRA jurisdiction and binding effect; this consequence counsels against loosening joint-employer findings absent exercised control because entities could be forced to adhere to CBAs they never negotiated or signed. (Citation 469.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Control over workplace safety does not necessarily establish joint-employer
rubrics_metrics.description: An entity's control or responsibility for workplace safety measures does not automatically prove a joint-employer relationship; courts have rejected the notion that safety control tends to prove joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA standards often allow alternative methods to satisfy duties; the existence of legally required safety duties complicates any carveout and may make the majority's safety-related carveout inapplicable. (Citations 491-493, 492 referencing OSHA regs and multiemployer citation policy.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory and statutory boundaries on agency rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: When promulgating rules under notice-and-comment (APA), the agency must provide a reasoned explanation, consider relevant factors, and rebut vital comments; rulemaking must 'color within the common-law lines identified by the judiciary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require agencies to respond meaningfully to significant public comments; failure to consider or rebut vital comments can render an agency action unreasoned under APA. (Citations 474, 466.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory flexibility and consideration of direct costs to small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency must accurately identify and quantify direct compliance costs imposed on small entities and describe steps to minimize significant economic impacts; misclassifying direct costs as indirect violates statutory obligations (5 U.S.C. 604(a)(6)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique that the majority misclassified costs (e.g., cost of evaluating contracts, placing bargaining reps) as indirect rather than direct and thus sidestepped required Regulatory Flexibility Analysis; AFL-CIO v. Chertoff discussed related obligations. (Citation 502.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical effect: increased litigation, bargaining delays, and enmeshment
rubrics_metrics.description: Relaxing the actual-exercise requirement risks rendering many more businesses joint employers (including neutral or previously uninvolved entities), leading to delays in collective bargaining, unfair-labor-practice charges, litigation, and increased exposure to picketing/secondary activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and comments predict substantial delay to bargaining and increased disputes; unions insisting on participation by putative joint employers could trigger unfair-labor-practice charges and protracted litigation. (Citations 471, 473, 501.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Retroactivity and scope consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a relaxed joint-employer standard retroactively means entities not previously identified as joint employers could be newly bound by collective-bargaining terms and duties, imposing unforeseen obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The potential retroactive application heightens the risk that many employers who never exercised control will be required to adhere to others' CBAs and assume bargaining obligations. (Citation 469.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/economic evidence for compliance-cost estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimates of time and cost for regulated entities to comply (e.g., one-hour reading estimate) must be supported by contemporaneous evidence and public comments; novel rules that 'break new legal ground' cannot rely on prior simpler estimates without justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent criticizes the majority's low estimate and cites public comments and industry data (e.g., Clio Legal Trends, Maloney article, Laffey/Fitzpatrick matrices) to show the estimate is unreasonably low. (Citations 503-507.)
